translations.text: Canons of Mar Rabbula, Bishop of Edessa.
First canon: Above all, monks must take care that women never enter their monasteries.
Furthermore, no monk is to give out oil, especially to women.
But if someone clearly possesses the gift, he may give oil to men. If there are women in need, it must be sent to them through their menfolk.
Furthermore, commemorations in monasteries must not involve gatherings of people, but only the brothers of the monastery itself.
Furthermore, monks must not leave their dwelling places, take on lawsuits on behalf of the poor, and go to cities or before judges.
Monks must not neglect the hours appointed for worship by day and by night on account of business [?] work.
Furthermore, no monk is to select passages from the Holy Scriptures for anyone.
Furthermore, if anyone buys grain for the monastery's needs, he must not take anything extra. Rather, at the price at which it is sold at the time
of threshing in that place, so he must buy it, without acting greedily in the monastery's name. Furthermore, as for diviners, charmers, and those who write amulets
and anoint men and women, operating under the guise of medical practice: drive them out of the entire region, and obtain a pledge from them that they will not enter our jurisdiction.
Furthermore, members of the church must not associate with heretics, either in word or in deed.
Here end the canons of Mar Rabbula, Bishop
of Edessa.
Admonitions concerning monks, by the very same Mar Rabbula, Bishop of Edessa.
Above all, monks must take care that women never enter their monasteries.
The brothers of the monastery must not enter villages, except for the monastery's steward alone, who must observe the discipline of modesty.
A steward who enters a village or city must not go around from house to house or spend the night in the homes of laypeople,
but in the church, or in a monastery if one is nearby. Monks must not drink wine, so that they do not blaspheme.
They must be especially diligent not to buy it and drink it. Monks must not let their hair grow long.
Nor may they wear iron or hang it on themselves, except for those who live in seclusion and never go out anywhere. Stewards who go out on the monastery's business
must not wear haircloth garments, nor may any of the brothers do so outside the monastery, so that they do not cheapen the dignity of the monastic habit.
No monk is to prepare oil, especially for women. But if there is someone who possesses the gift
manifestly, he may give oil to men. If there are women in need, it must be sent to them through their menfolk.
Commemorations in monasteries must not involve gatherings of people, but only the brothers of the monastery itself.
Monks must not own sheep or goats, horses or mules, or any other livestock, except for one donkey for those who need it,
or one yoke of oxen for those who cultivate the land. Books that are outside the faith of the Church must not be kept in monasteries.
There must be no buying and selling as a business in monasteries, except only what is sufficient for their needs, without greed.
None of the brothers living in monasteries may own anything privately for himself, apart from what belongs to the brotherhood in common and is under the abbot’s authority.
Abbots must not allow the brothers to meet with their relatives or to go out and visit them, so that they do not grow lax.
The brothers must not leave their monasteries under the pretext of illness and wander about in towns or villages.
Instead, they must endure their afflictions within their monasteries for the love of God.
Monks must not leave their dwelling places and stir up lawsuits on behalf of others, going to towns or appearing before judges.
Monks must not neglect the times appointed for worship by day and by night on account of business or work.
They must welcome strangers lovingly and must not shut the door against any of the brothers. None of the brothers may live alone, except
someone who has demonstrated the quality of his conduct over a long period. No monk may draw a verse from Scripture for anyone.
None of the brothers who is not a priest or deacon may presume to distribute Holy Communion. Those who have become priests and deacons in monasteries,
and have been entrusted with churches in villages, must appoint abbots in their monasteries from among those who have proved themselves and are able to govern the brotherhood.
They themselves must attend diligently to their churches. Martyrs’ bones must not be kept in monasteries. Whoever has any must bring [?] them before us,
so that, if they are genuine, they may be honored in a martyrs’ shrine; but if not, they must be placed in a cemetery.
Any burial sarcophagi that monks wish to make for themselves must be buried in the ground so that they cannot be seen at all.
If a brother or the abbot of one of the monasteries departs from this world, only the brothers of that monastery are to bury him, quietly.
If they are not sufficient, they may call brothers from a nearby monastery to join them. They must not gather people from the villages or laypeople for the funeral procession.
If anyone buys grain for the monastery’s needs, he must not take anything extra, but must buy it at the price for which it is being sold at that threshing season,
without acting greedily in the monastery’s name. No one may receive a brother who moves from one monastery to another without the permission of the abbot with whom he was living.
The admonitions for monks are completed.
Commands and Admonitions for Priests and Members of the Covenant, by Mar Rabbula, Bishop of Edessa.
Above all, the members of the Church must know the true faith of the holy Church, so that heretics do not lead them astray.
No visiting church official, priest, deacon, or member of the Covenant may live with women, except with his mother,
his sister, or his daughter. They must not house these women separately from themselves and then be constantly visiting them.
Priests, deacons, and sons of the covenant must not force daughters of the covenant to weave clothing for them.
Priests and deacons must not have women serve them, especially daughters of the covenant.
Priests, deacons, and itinerant overseers must not accept bribes from anyone, especially from those who have a legal case.
Priests and deacons must not impose levies on sons of the covenant or on laypeople, even if they are ordered to do so by
the city authorities. Instead, the church's needs must be met by those who give voluntarily.
When the bishop goes to a village, they must not impose levies on the laypeople in the bishop's name.
Instead, if they incur expenses at the church, they must provide what is sufficient from the church's own resources. But if the church has nothing, they must give nothing.
Priests must not demand gifts for festivals or memorial services by pressuring anyone to give anything under compulsion. Instead, they must leave it to the giver's own choice.
Priests, deacons, sons of the covenant, and daughters of the covenant must not seek interest, fixed loan charges, or any occupation yielding shameful profits.
Their priests must not allow sons or daughters of the covenant to live with laypeople, but only with their own relatives or with one another.
All you members of the church, be constant in fasting and diligent in prayer. Care for the poor and seek justice for the oppressed without showing favoritism.
All you priests in the villages, care for the poor who come to you and provide them with relief,
especially those who are sons of the covenant. Itinerant overseers must not present a man who has a blemish for the rank of priesthood,
nor those who are under the yoke of slavery and have not been freed. Instead, act as the apostle commanded.
Itinerant overseers must not entrust the hearing of legal cases to just anyone, but to people who have been shown by experience not to show favoritism.
Priests and deacons must bear responsibility for the monasteries in their territories. Care for them
as for your own bodily members. Also encourage the laypeople to share with them in these material needs.
Women must not go inside the gates of their monasteries. At every church,
one house must be designated where the poor who come there can find rest.
Drive out of the whole region diviners, enchanters, and those who inscribe metal plates and measure men and women, operating under the guise of medicine.
Take guarantees from them that they will not enter our jurisdiction. Daughters of the covenant must not be allowed to come to church or go out at night individually.
If possible, they should live together. The same applies to sons of the covenant. If any sons or daughters of the covenant are in need,
the priests or deacons of their village must take responsibility for their care. If this is beyond his means, he must inform us so that we may attend to their needs,
lest, because of their [?], they be compelled to do something improper. Sons of the covenant must learn the Psalms,
and daughters of the covenant must also learn hymns. Priests, deacons, sons of the covenant, and daughters of the covenant must not utter God's name in swearing oaths.
Not over a falsehood or over the truth, but as commanded. Church visitors must not lodge
—nor must priests or deacons—in lodging houses or taverns when they enter a city.
Instead, they must lodge in the church's guesthouse or in the monasteries outside. Priests, deacons, and sons
of the covenant, and daughters of the covenant, must abstain from wine and meat. But if any of them is physically weak, he may use a little, as it is written. Those who get drunk or enter taverns,
however, must be expelled from the church. All who have become disciples of Christ must not be eager to acquire more than they need,
but must distribute it to the poor. Priests, deacons, and sons of the covenant must not serve as guardians or administrators for laypeople,
or take upon themselves the lawsuits of their relatives, or undertake anyone's lawsuits for pay, or frequent the judge's gate...
Priests, deacons, sons of the covenant, and daughters of the covenant must be constant in the church's services. They must not neglect the appointed times for prayer and psalms, by night or by day.
Excommunicate, imprison, and send to the judge in the city any layman who dares to take a daughter of the covenant. But if she too was defiled with her consent,
send her as well. Sons or daughters of the covenant who fall from their rank must be lodged in monasteries for repentance.
But if they do not remain in the monastery, they must not be received in the church. Instead, they must remain under restriction with their parents for as long as is appropriate.
They must not receive into discipleship a married woman without her husband, or a married man without his wife,
so that God's name will not be blasphemed. Priests must not allow [?] those who are found
in sexual immorality to receive Communion, except by our command. No priest, deacon, or member of the church
may dare to put ordinary vessels beside the sacred vessels in a chest or case.
No one may dare to approach and administer Communion unless he is a priest or deacon. Treat all village lords with the honor due to them,
without showing them favoritism and wronging the poor. Do not flog anyone.
But if there is a matter that makes flogging necessary, either flog only enough to frighten, or send the offenders to the secular judges.
Settle lawsuits, so that people do not come and wear themselves out in litigation. Send before us those whose cases are beyond you.
They must not allow sons of the covenant to go to gatherings or other places without priests, nor daughters of the covenant without deaconesses.
No priest, deacon, or son of the covenant may travel to the imperial court or to a distant place and leave his church without our command,
not even on business concerning his village or his church. All priests must attend to the service of God's house.
Do everything required for the upkeep of the house. Do not feed animals in the church, so that God's house is not dishonored.
A church visitor, priest, or deacon who departs this world must leave whatever he has to the church.
Priests, deacons, and sons of the covenant must not act as guarantors for anyone in writing.
Nor without a written document. Priests and deacons are to live at the church, and, if possible, members of the covenant as well.
Priests and deacons are to take care that a copy of the separate Gospels is available and read in every church.
Where priests are present, they, and not deacons, are to read the Gospel. Likewise, wherever priests are present, the sign of the cross
is to be given by the priests themselves. Laypeople are not to serve as stewards in the church, except where there are no suitable members of the covenant.
Members of the clergy and women of the covenant are not to drink wine in mourning for the dead.
You are not to accept a payment [?] from anyone and, because of it, do anything contrary to justice.
Members of the church are not to associate with heretics, either in word or in deed. They are not to allow any heretic to live in a monastery.
None of the heretics who come to church while remaining divided in their convictions is to approach Holy Communion. Search everywhere for the books and scrolls of heretics.
Wherever you find them, either bring them to us or burn them in the fire. Heretics are not to be admitted to baptism without examination.
Instead, they are to demonstrate that they have been tested, and then be admitted. Priests are not to give Communion to those afflicted by demons,
so that the holy sacrament is not dishonored through fellowship with demons. Cut down the trees that were dedicated to demons,
and let them provide for the expenses of the church in their locality. If any remnant of an idol temple stands in a place, let it be uprooted [?] without disturbance. Churches—
build them wherever there are none. Those already built are to be whitewashed, and they are to have sanctuaries and securely enclosed courtyards.
No member of the church upon whom the name of Christ has been invoked is to dare to castrate himself.
A man is not to leave his wife unless he has found her committing adultery. Nor is a woman to leave her husband on one pretext or another.
No one is to marry his sister’s daughter or his brother’s daughter, nor his maternal aunt or paternal aunt. Members of the [?] are not to go up onto the altar platform.
No food is to be brought up into the sanctuary, nor are priests to eat there, nor is anyone to chew food in the church hall. Nothing is to be placed there except the sacred vessels.
When priests and deacons give Holy Communion, they are not to accept any gift from those receiving it.
Here end the commandments and admonitions addressed to priests
and members of the covenant.
A letter of Mar Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, to Andrew of Samosata.
To my lord Andrew, the bishop honored in every way and beloved of God, from Rabbula. Although I have been eager to meet your God-fearing Reverence, sometimes an illness that befell my body,
sometimes the severity of winter, and at other times the inactivity of your God-fearing Reverence have prevented me. For perhaps, although we loved one another in every respect,
we have delayed making contact through news from afar. But now a certain document that has come into our hands has compelled us to write to your God-fearing Reverence.
[?] It contains a refutation of twelve chapters that are said to have been composed by the God-fearing bishop Cyril.
At first, then, I thought that the book belonged to the honored Nestorius, because the things for which we all commonly blamed him
were plainly present in it. But when some people insisted that it belonged to your Holiness, we were astonished. I therefore thought it right to write this very thing, and through
what your Modesty writes, I will learn. The division of the natures has greatly disturbed me [?], especially after the union.
For it introduces two sons for us instead of one, as the remarkable Anastasius said in the midst of Constantinople:
“I confess the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and our Lord Jesus Christ.” I am so far from accepting all this
that I would gladly endure anything rather than share in any such blasphemy.
From Andrew to Mar Rabbula
To my lord, the wholly God-fearing, holy and reverend Bishop Rabbula: Andrew sends greetings in our Lord.
Someone came from there some time ago and informed us that your God-fearing Reverence was using many insults against us,
and not only privately, but publicly as well. He added that you had even pronounced an anathema before the church.
And after other things: When we hear, “In the beginning was the Word,” and, “He was in the world, and the world came into being through him,”
and, “The radiance of his glory and the image of the Father's being,” and all such expressions, it is the Father's only Son, who existed from
before the ages, whom we understand. But when we read in turn, “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,”
and, “The child grew and became strong in spirit,” and, “Jesus grew in stature and wisdom,” and that God highly exalted him
and gave him the name that is above every name, and anything else like these expressions, we apply them to the one descended from Abraham.
And after other things: The form of God and the form of a servant; the flesh and the Word; the temple and its inhabitant.
But if he speaks of God alone, without our understanding the human being together with him, and again if we do not see the one who is in him, we necessarily remove one.
And after other things: Someone from among the pagans approaches, wishing to learn our teaching. What should the teacher say to him
to instruct him about Christ? What, then, is right? That he exists only in the form of God and is equal to God,

but did not take the form of a servant for our sake? Then let us deny God's plan altogether! Rather, let us teach that he is God, who clothed himself in [?] a human being for our sake. The letter is finished.
A portion of the letter of the blessed Rabbula written to the blessed Cyril
For there was a certain bishop from the region of Cilicia, a man who spoke persuasively and was capable of convincing people.
Some things he expounded from the pulpit in a way that pleased the people; but other things, which are a deadly snare, he set down in writings.
At the beginnings of these writings of his, he bound those who read them under an anathema not to reveal to others what was written in them.
He laid this down first: that the holy Virgin is not the Mother of God, as though God the Word had not accepted a birth like ours.
Although this had escaped notice until now, so that it would not seem powerful by becoming established over a long time,
through God's action, when Nestorius, the leader of the new sect, went astray, he exposed it openly.
Letter of the blessed Cyril to Mar Rabbula.
To my holy lord, our brother and fellow minister, Bishop Rabbula: Cyril, bishop, sends greetings in our Lord.
The blessed Paul arms our souls with unconquerable strength and unfailing courage when he writes as follows:
"Who will separate me from the love of Christ? Affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?"
For there is nothing that those who have resolved to fight the good fight of faith cannot endure, so that they may finish their race, keep their faith, and receive an imperishable crown.
For just as those who know how to steer ships skillfully are recognized, not when they sail in calm weather, but when they save their ship amid storms,
as being skilled sailors, so also those who have undertaken to govern the holy churches
distinguish themselves not when affairs are peaceful; rather, their skill becomes known through trials, endurance, and diligence,
and when they stand firmly against the shameful inventions that heretics devise out of their own hearts. Your Holiness, my lord, has therefore distinguished yourself at all times,
but especially at this time, when you have become a pillar and foundation of the truth for all the inhabitants of the East. And as
though pursuing a deadly disease, you pursue the abominable blasphemies of Nestorius that have now sprung up, which have sprouted from another root.
I mean from Theodore, the one who was in Cilicia. For this impiety began there.
He imagined that he would rule over the whole earth because of the authority that—I do not know how—was given to him.
For he seized the great throne and became food for the many-headed dragon. He imagined that he too would swallow up the church of God,
who brings all things into subjection. Had God, who is over all, not rescued us, perhaps, just as this wicked man imagined that she had fallen into his hands,
and in keeping with the zeal of his supporters, his wish would have been fulfilled. But, as the prophet said, "Our God is with us.
Know this, nations, and be defeated, you who are strong! For even if you strengthen yourselves again, you will again be defeated.
Every plan you devise, the Lord will frustrate, and every scheme you conceive will not stand, because the Lord our God is with us."
For this reason God himself stands in defense of those who proclaim his truth, and he shakes and overthrows the strength of their opponents.
He turns their schemes against them, and they do not come to fulfillment as they expect. Therefore, do not let those who, as is their habit,
shamelessly and senselessly threaten everyone intimidate Your Perfection with their threats, since they have become servants of the blasphemies of Nestorius.
For they have no priestly authority whatsoever, because the holy synod has annulled everything they dare
to do to anyone, as have, collectively, all the holy bishops within the Roman Empire.
We are united with your illustrious Eminence in mind, will, zeal, concord, fellowship, and faith.
For you distinguish yourself in this way, and through your wise teaching you strengthen those who are under your authority,
as well as those who live in other cities and regions. And it is not only those who are near your Holiness,
but also those who are far away whom you instruct. As for the reproaches from the wicked, the insults, and the other disputes,
I am not greatly troubled. For if they called our Lord Beelzebul, it is nothing new if they call us that too.
And if they persecuted him, how would they not persecute us? But in all these things we are victorious, and our suffering causes the fruits of Christ’s love to increase.
It also makes us share in glory that does not pass away. For your Perfection, wise in everything, is capable of guiding the regions near you
along the straight path and teaching the message of faith purely and accurately. But because some people go astray and proclaim the teaching of error
that recently sprang up through Nestorius, taking innocent people captive and leading them astray,
I too, out of necessity and as far as my strength allowed, set out an argument against his error, as was fitting.
And I wrote it in a [?], refuting his blasphemies by the power of the truth. I also sent it to your Holiness, asking you to be willing
to condescend to correct in it anything that escaped our notice. And if it seems helpful, arrange for these writings to be read before the faithful brothers as well.
I also wrote a discourse on the incarnation of the Son of God, in the person of the faithful emperor, which I sent to your Eminence.
And if it seems to you that you should also read this to the faithful brothers, do as you see fit. For I too read the letters sent by your Perfection before all the clergy
and to the bishops who were received here with us in Alexandria, showing them that Christ is not inactive, but has lights everywhere
who speak [?] of life. And whenever your Perfection wishes, what is written in those books refutes those who insult us,
claiming that we say God’s nature is subject to suffering, or that we hold the opinion of Apollinaris or of other heretics.
For when you examine them carefully, your Holiness will understand that the meaning of the propositions we set out has been correctly explained throughout the book.
Through this, too, the arrows shot against us from insolent mouths will be rendered ineffective. These things are sufficient for God’s [?] in you.
By Saint Rabbula, bishop of Edessa. From the letter to Gemellinus, bishop of Perrha.
For those who eat the holy bread in faith eat, in it and with it, the living body of God who sanctifies. But those who eat it without faith
receive food, like the other things the body needs. For if that bread is seized and forcibly eaten by enemies,
they eat ordinary bread, because those who eat it do not have the faith that perceives its sweetness.
For the palate tastes the bread, but faith tastes the power hidden in the bread. For what is eaten is not by itself the body of our Life-giver,
as we said a little earlier, but that which is shared with it, where we have faith.
For a power that cannot be eaten is united with bread that can be eaten, and it becomes one for those who receive it, just as
the hidden names are united with the visible water, and from them comes birth anew.
For the Spirit hovers invisibly over the visible water, to bring forth from it anew the likeness of the heavenly [?].
From a letter of Rabbula to Gamalinus, bishop of Perrha, concerning those who abuse the mysteries and feed on them as though they were ordinary bread.
I have heard that in your region of Perrha there are some among the brothers who do not understand their way of life.
And others among the heads of monasteries and the ministers there have falsely claimed for themselves the empty reputation of not eating bread.
They have falsely laid claim to the empty boast that they do not drink water, and have described themselves as abstaining from wine.
So, when I heard that they were abusing the body and blood of the Son of God, Jesus, who was mentioned, I [?].
But because the compulsion of [?] has overcome us, I dare to say these things: that the very thing they do not tremble to do to the body and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord,
we have approached it madly and without discernment. That is, the body
that is holy and makes holy those who receive it, and the blood[?] that is living and gives life to those who drink it.
These are the people who—I do not know how they can do this [?]—wickedly satisfy from it, they say, their nature’s constant need arising from hunger and thirst.
They cannot bear to go voluntarily even a single day without the offering. Rather, every day a large part of their nourishment regularly comes from the consecrated elements.
For this reason, they also leaven the dough they prepare lavishly, refine it with great effort,
and bake it carefully, so that it will serve them as food, rather than as the mystery of Christ’s body, which is represented by unleavened bread.
And the rest, they say, whenever they recline to eat, also place ordinary, unconsecrated bread in one another’s hands and eat it. And sometimes, they say, when they travel from place to place
or go on a long journey, twice or three times in a single day
they satisfy their natural hunger and thirst from it—from the very body of our Lord. And when they stop at the place they reach,
in the evening, they say, they offer the offering again and receive from it as though they had been fasting. Even during the holy days of the forty-day fast,
they dare to act this way, without fear of God or shame before people. And people who, as we have said,
partake of bread and water every day are found eating holy bread and drinking consecrated wine
on glorious days like these, when even fools abstain. But the Spirit within me is my witness, holy brother, that I hesitate
to write to Your Honor everything I have heard about them, because I could not bring my conscience to believe that these things were really true.
And if it had been possible for you to learn what I wish to teach without a letter or a word from me,
and for these people to receive guidance through your correction, I would have wished neither you, my lord, nor they to know that anything at all had been heard about them.

Do not, then, think—and let them not suppose—that I wrote these things to you about them because I believed the bad report concerning them. Rather, while I am still uncertain, I speak to others as well.
For it is impossible that so great a sin as this should ever be committed by those baptized into Christ. For they say that, when they have celebrated the sacrament in a basket,
they freely eat as much of it as they want. As for the cup of blood, each of them mixes it [?] with as much hot water as they can, like diluted wine, and drinks.
Then he fills it again and gives it to his companion, so that, because of the great quantity of wine they drink in the name of the sacrament,
they are often compelled even to spew it out of their mouths. Or this, which is no less serious, if it is true: the precious sacred vessels,

which are awe-inspiring because of the mysteries within them, and which even rational beings are afraid to approach boldly—these men, at the peril of their lives, have handed them over and made them vessels for serving their bellies. They did not even remember the punishment that Belshazzar, the pagan king, received, and how he was rebuked,
because he intended to insult God through the vessels used in his service,
and acted as a rebel against God by using them contemptuously. The likeness of the palm of a writing hand was sent from on high to write on the wall of his house
the righteous sentence of his mercy. But how can the vessels used in the service of the temple in Jerusalem be compared
with the glorious vessels used in the service of the body and blood of the Son of God? For not even the bread of the Presence belonging to the priests of Israel
is worthy to be compared in any way with the glory of the exalted mystery. And if anyone compares that bread from the table, which David ate when he was hungry,
with the life-giving body of God the Word, we ought to regard him as a foolish person who does not distinguish the body and blood of the Lord from the bread of the Presence.
For this reason he is guilty concerning the body and blood of our Lord. For that bread scarcely cleansed bodily defilement, even when various kinds of washings were joined to it,
along with the observance of various rules. But this life-giving body and blood of the Lord Jesus not only forgives the sins of soul and body and sanctifies those who receive it in faith,
but also causes God himself to be in us: he through his Spirit, just as we are in him through our body.
“Whoever eats my body and drinks my blood,” says the Son of God, “is in me, and I am in him. I will raise him up on the last day.”
Again, in another way [?], we can understand the greatness of this new ministry, handed down to us by God the Word, from the harsh and severe punishment that Paul decreed against those
who indulged themselves in it—a punishment greater than what we understand those who transgress the old ministry, handed down by Moses, receive. For he said:
“If someone who transgressed the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses,
how much more bitter a punishment would someone deserve who trampled on the Son of God, regarded the blood of his covenant as something common to everyone,
and insulted the Spirit of his grace, by which we were sanctified?” This, then, is the bread of life that came down from heaven and gives life to the world because of its union with God the Word.
Who is so mad as to compare it with the bread of the Presence, [?] from the earth? Yet the thinking of someone who thinks or acts in this way has become known and is again plainly apparent:
in practice he has counted it as ordinary bread, just as it appears to the person who receives it so foolishly and does not believe the Son, who said,
“The bread that I will give is my body, which is given for the life of the world.” Therefore, in the body of Christ there is not merely bread,
as it appears to them; rather, in the bread is the body of the invisible God, as we believe, and we readily receive it as the body [?].
They readily eat what is fine and refined. They use cheese instead of bread, it is said.
With fish, too, in every flavor, their cravings find satisfaction. They take great delight in fresh fruit and enjoy dried fruit even more,
along with honey cakes and egg fritters. And because the heat of the wine they drink in the name of holiness inflames their thirst even more,

throughout the summer, when sheep’s and goats’ milk is available, they continually drink it. They have done this deliberately, for they have discovered that the moisture of the bread of the offering [?] enables them to relieve
the burning that continually comes from wine in their dissipation. Concerning these things and on their account, in due course
God’s just rebuke, which he addressed to Eli because of his sons, will be quoted as applying to them too:
“Look, I have given you all the good things of the earth so that you may use them without sin.

Just as I set apart for them all the offerings of the Israelites so that they might enjoy them without blame, why have you also acted wickedly toward my body and my blood, like those who acted wrongfully toward my sacrifices and my offerings?”
Although the wrong these men do to God far exceeds the wrong those men did to the people, there would be lamentation and great trembling, if they had any feeling,
lest a punishment like the one pronounced against those men should also be decreed against them. “Therefore,” he says, “thus says the Lord, the God of Israel:
I did indeed say that your house and your father’s house would serve before me forever. But now, says the Lord, far be it from me! For I will honor those who honor me,
and those who despise me will be disgraced.” Do you see how he rejected them from the priesthood forever and made them outcasts and strangers to his house?
But what shall I say about these men, who neither measure up to the prophets of the Old Testament nor resemble the apostles of the New?
It would have been right for them at least to learn from Peter, the chief of the apostles, what his food was. For he stated
plainly what sustained his bodily life. When Clement, his chosen disciple, asked him to allow him alone to attend to his needs,
he spoke to him as follows, praising his eagerness and making little of his own fare: “For who,” he said, “can manage all this service?
Do we not continually eat bread and olives, and, if it happens sometime, also accept vegetables?”
Nor, again, have they received the good tradition from Paul, the herald of truth. For he too, because of his great need, sent and sold his tunic.
It is written that with its proceeds they bought only bread and brought it to him along with vegetables, so that by his conduct he might establish a rule for us too,
just as by his words: “If we have food and clothing, this is enough for us.” And if it is beneath them to imitate the apostles, the pillars of the world,
let them at least emulate the Lord of the apostles, the maker of the worlds and everything in them! But perhaps even our God’s life as a human being is contemptible and despised in their eyes.
For everywhere our Lord showed us that it was bread he ate—and bread not even of wheat, but of barley.
And seven other loaves, which multiplied and increased at his word: four thousand people ate from them
and left seven baskets full of bread. And when he ate the Passover with his disciples, unleavened bread was set before him.
Even after his resurrection from the dead, he ate bread with his disciples for forty days, so that they might believe in our Lord’s human life and his tangible bodily existence. Just as
For they too wrote that Jesus used to go in and out among them, and went to the house of Cleopas, though he did not wish them to recognize him while he was walking with them on the road.
He blessed the bread and broke it for them inside the house, and then they recognized him.
But these people, as I hear from you, follow those who go astray in their deeds, and do not conform to the truth in their conduct either. For they are not celibate like the Marcionites.
Nor are they ascetics like the Christians. Indeed, they do not resemble even those unbelievers who eat only flour or bread.
And they do not practice falsehood concerning their offerings. Nor, indeed, does anyone grant the faithful this: that we eat ordinary bread in measured amounts,
and receive the medicine of our true life with discernment. Why have these gluttons not trained themselves to be satisfied with only small amounts?

And why have these dissolute people not accustomed themselves to filling their bellies with something cheap and humble? And why do they not eat bread alone, which is readily available, simple, and inexpensive?
But it is clear that [?], so that they will not suffer hardship. (If) But if they truly wish to afflict their bodies, they should not eat their fill even when eating bread alone.
And look: they have become corrupted, wasted away, and defiled. But it is plain and well known that these people are not fighting against their bodies.
Nor do they even contend with Satan. Rather, they labor for worthless praise through the devices of their evil tricks,
and not through the hardships of asceticism. The rest of the letter likewise contains proofs from the Scriptures.
A sermon delivered by Mar Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, in the church of Constantinople before all the people.
We are small in our speech and knowledge, but you are great in the wisdom of the Spirit and in eloquence of language.
Therefore, who would not tremble in a church like this? For it is a very weighty matter for unlearned people to judge the words of a learned man.
But this is what I have been praying and asking of God: that everyone should be made wise in this way through the gift of the Spirit that we have in our hearts,
so that no one would need instruction from another. For grace is the fountain of all teaching,
through which our Lord was [?] and singing to his church. For although we possessed knowledge by nature,
sin nevertheless reigned over us through our own will and darkened our understanding. For this reason the gift of the written law came,
so that, by seeing this visible thing, the hidden thing that lies within us might be awakened in us. But because the people of earlier times, in turn, lived their lives carelessly,
they became dead in their bodies to what belonged to nature, and buried what belonged to the law in their souls. For because of the weakness of their flesh,
they could not carry out in deeds what they knew by nature and were reminded of by the law.
But when the grace of God Almighty appeared to all humanity, it trained us through the wisdom that comes from it
to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires, and to live in this world with self-control, righteousness, and reverence for God.
For our Lord’s saving work and his suffering, which is the salvation of us all, gave us true help that strengthens us in our weakness,
so that we would possess not only knowledge, but also the strength to carry out his commandments. These things are enough, my brothers, if you are willing to be persuaded.
So abandon all pursuit of investigations and disputes over words, and let us eagerly hasten to perform the deeds required of us.
For today it is not right for us to bind our whole mind to excessive inquiry and disputes over words.
For it is mockery and a great insult for someone to debate God's greatness insolently and without fear.
For it was Satan who envied our former honor and, through his enticements, cast us out of our delightful dwelling.
Even today he is jealous of the latter salvation that has come to us, seeking through his temptations to cast us down even from the height of heaven.
For it is he who, through his schemes, turns us away from carrying out our Lord's commandments,
which can unite us to him through the fellowship that comes from him. But toward difficult inquiry that exceeds our capacity
he draws us, to deprive us of our life. It is helpful, however, for someone to acquire knowledge in due measure, enough to spur him on to good deeds.

Likewise, it is good for us to look at the sun with [?], so that from the beauty of what was made we may understand the excellence of its Maker. But if someone insists on gazing at the sun beyond what is proper,
not only does he fail to see it as he wishes, but through his rashness he also damages his eyesight.
I wished to speak to God's church about virtuous conduct—not because it needs my teaching,
a countryman who lives among country people. For, as a rule, we speak Syriac.
What, then, shall we teach an assembly like this, which is itself capable of teaching everyone?
There are two chief commandments, my beloved, in which the Law and the Prophets are summed up. The first is that you should love the Lord your God
with all your heart. Whoever loves, then, does not investigate but obeys, and does not inquire except through deeds.
For he says, “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments.” The other, the second, which is like it, is that you should love your neighbor as yourself.
Again, whoever loves does not murder, does not steal, does not commit adultery, nor does he lie or mistreat anyone. For whatever he does not want anyone to do to him,
he does not do to others. Rather, whatever he wants people to do to him,
he likewise does to them, because he loves them. These, my brothers, are the teachings that benefit our souls, and what is useful
for building up the whole church of Christ. Therefore we ought always to devote ourselves to them in our deeds.
For they alone are the good substance of our true righteousness. But because I know that your readiness to listen, together with the understanding of your minds,
looks toward our word and our faith and waits to hear, and is eager to know our truth in Christ, your love compels us to speak before you
of things that ought to be honored only in the silence of faith. This, then, is the question you are asking:
whether the Virgin Mary is truly the Mother of God, or is called this in name only, or perhaps ought not even to be given this title.
But as for us, our hope is firm—for he is also our life—and our trust is secure—for he is also our boast.
We declare aloud, without denial, that Mary is the Mother of God.
And she is rightly proclaimed as such, for by his will she became the earthly mother of God the Word,
who by nature had no mother in heaven. For the apostle cries out, “God sent his Son, and he came to be from a woman.”
But if anyone dares to say that she gave birth to God the Word by nature, not only does he speak incorrectly, but he also makes an impious confession.
For we call the holy Virgin the Mother of God, not because she gave birth to the divinity by nature, but because God the Word was born from her when he became human.
For it says, “Look, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel,” which means “Our God is with us.” But [?]
as though our Lord acquired his first beginning from the blessed Virgin. For the Word was in the beginning with his Father, according to John's testimony.
Rather, it was because Christ, who is by nature God over all, appeared from her in the flesh because of his mercy.
Forgive us, my beloved, for the brevity of our discourse. For we do not speak by following an author's teachings.
For it is not our custom to write our homily beforehand, learn it, and then recite it.
Rather, whatever grace brings forth in our mind is what we speak to God's people without preparation.
But we ask you, my brothers, to consider intelligently the meaning of our plain discourse, rather than the arrangement of polished words.
We believe, then, that God the Word was with God and was begotten by nature from the Father from eternity.
But at the end of the ages, for our salvation, he was born in the flesh from the Virgin. Therefore, those who suppose that he was born by nature from the Virgin do not
confess rightly. Nor can those who say that Mary gave birth to a mere human being, or to someone anointed by the Spirit,
escape blasphemy, even if they offer the excuse that, because of disputes against heretics, they refrain from proclaiming
that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God. But we believe, according to the confession of our holy fathers, that God the Word became incarnate and became human for our sake.
It was not one person in another, but one: he who is eternally with the Father, from the Father's nature. He himself was born in the flesh
from the offspring of the house of David, from the holy Virgin, the Mother of God, without losing what he was: God, Son, and Only Begotten.
Rather, even when he became human, he remained God in his nature, Son in his person, and the Only Begotten in number, as well as the Firstborn in his humanity.
No addition or diminution involving any change happened to him. Although he is by nature incapable of suffering,
his own body suffered by his will. For the Only Begotten himself, having become a priest, offered himself to his Father on our behalf as a sacrifice without blemish.
And he gave us life through his death on our behalf. For just as he fought Satan in his body, defeated him, and subjected him beneath our feet, he also suffered [?]
Again we write supplications of every kind in the eight tones, from the first to the eighth.
First. First order. First, for the Mother of God. Hail to you, holiest of all, Mary, Mother of God, the splendid and precious treasure of the whole inhabited world.
Brightly burning lamp and palace of the [?] One, pure temple of the Creator of all creation, hail to you! In your hands he became known,
he who takes away the sin of the world and saves it. Another hymn. On the mountains of Horeb, Moses the prophet saw you as a wonder, holy Virgin.
Fire dwelt inside the bush and blazed in it, yet the bush did not burn. You were also prefigured
by the ladder that righteous Jacob saw in the wilderness, on which the watchers ascended to heaven and descended. Likewise, the son of Jesse
took up his spiritual harp and began to proclaim with it: Just as gentle [?] rain falls upon the earth, so God descended and dwelt
in the Virgin. Now let the young women and the Hebrew virgins come with their tambourines in their hands, and let them play through the Holy Spirit before the King's Son.
Let them say to you, “Blessed are you, Mary, for you gave birth to our Lord [?].” Of the martyrs. You appeared as speaking clusters of grapes, blessed martyrs.
The Church was refreshed by your wine, O glorious and divine lights, who joyfully offered battle against every affliction.
Through your heroic struggle you conquered the accursed tyrants and put them to shame. Glory to the power that strengthened you in your contests.
God, who came to save his creatures, have mercy on us. When the holy ones entered and reclined at the banquet of sufferings,
they all drank from that wine which the people pressed at Golgotha, and they learned the hidden mysteries of God's house.
Therefore we sing praises and say: Blessed is Christ, who gave the holy martyrs their fill of the blood from his side.
Of repentance. O you who abound in mercy and compassion, O cleanser of the stains of all sinners, wash me with your pure hyssop and have mercy on me.
As you did for the tax collector and that sinful woman, show me compassion in your mercy. Christ, pardon sinners their offenses.
For you are the one who welcomes all who repent. Savior of our human race, save me in your mercy. If the righteous person is scarcely saved,
what shall I do, sinner that I am? For I have not endured the burden of the day or the scorching heat of the sun.
But count me among those laborers of the eleventh hour, Savior, and have mercy on me. My sins have overthrown me.
They have brought me down from the height where I once stood, and I have slipped toward destruction as into a pit. Who will once again restore to me the splendid
beauty, unless it is you, the skillful Creator, who fashioned me from the beginning in your image and likeness?
Yet I willingly became Satan's companion and a slave to sin. In your mercy, my Lord, set me free and have mercy on me. Of the departed.
Lord, clothe the bodies of the departed who put you on in baptism with a robe of glory when you come, when, at the sound of the horn and trumpet,
you will raise and renew our entire race. My Lord, forgive their offenses and remove their sins in the abundance of your grace.
Glory to the power of your being, Lord of lords. God, who came to save his creatures, give life to your servants.
When Jesus our Savior entered the city of the dead, a great tumult was heard in Sheol, and its foundations trembled.
Those dwelling in the graves longed for him when they saw his light shining upon them. He rose to life in glory and raised us with him.
And for this we sing praises and say: Blessed is he who raises the dead and renews the mortal race once more from corruption.
Jesus our Savior will come on wheels of fire in great glory, when he comes to bring about a new resurrection of the departed who have fallen asleep in hope of him.
The Judge will sit, and the generations will come before him for righteous judgment. Then he will open his books.
The good will rejoice and delight in eternal life. My Lord, on the day of your coming, make your servants who have fallen asleep in hope of you worthy of that life.
May they not be banished from the sight of you in your divinity, O greatly merciful one. Rather, may they offer you new praise when you come,
O lover of humanity. Of the Resurrection. My Lord, you were nailed to the cross by wicked men, and by stretching out both your hands,
you took hold of the four quarters of the world. The sun grew dark in the sky when it saw you, my Lord, naked [?].
At midday, in broad daylight, night came and established its rule. With the cry you uttered on the tree, you shook earth and heaven.
In your mercy you were counted among the dead, and you rose from the tomb because you willed it. You raised Adam with you and returned him to Eden,
from which he had departed. Your grace is good, Lord. Lord of all, glory to you. End of the [?] of Rabbula the bishop.
